guard.G46.why.1: The same alert came again. Whatever number it is, if I didn't start it, block it.
guard.G46.why.2: The third alert. Pestering you into tapping once is the trick, so block it.
guard.G46.why.3: It keeps coming, but the answer is the same. Block it.
guard.G46.why.4: In the morning Ria tapped the sign-in button herself. Approve this alert.
guard.G46.why.5: Ria was watering the plants and didn't sign in. Block it.
guard.G46.why.6: Yesterday's sign-in is already over. This alert wasn't started by me, so block it.
guard.G46.why.7: The alert came during lunch, so block it.
guard.G46.why.8: Ria just tapped the sign-in button again. Approve it.
guard.G46.why.9: The alert came while Ria was out at the market, so block it.
guard.G47.brief: Every call today claims to be from the "Gaon Investigation Office". Each attempt brings what the caller asked for, as one word. If it is a request that moves money ('transfer' a bank transfer, 'safe_account' a transfer to a "safe account", 'cash_pickup' handing over cash), return False (likely scam); for any other notice return True. The asks_money function decides whether it is a money request.
guard.G47.concept: Government impersonation: unlike G3, which blocks a list of guessable passwords, this blocks requests that move money and splits that decision into the function asks_money
guard.G47.crowIntro: "This is the Gaon Investigation Office~ move your money to a safe account~" Just lower my voice and you'll believe it, right?
guard.G47.crowLose: I even played the investigator and got caught right away!
guard.G47.file.real: Scammers pose as prosecutors, police, or financial regulators, scare you by saying you are "involved in a crime," then tell you to move money to prove you are innocent.
guard.G47.file.todo: Real investigators never ask you to move money by phone or messenger. Hang up and call the agency's official number yourself.
guard.G47.ria: Real investigators never tell you to move money over the phone. The asks_money function decides whether money is being asked for, and check returns the opposite of its answer.
guard.G47.title: A Call from the Gaon Investigation Office
guard.G47.why.0: They claim to be an agency and ask for a transfer. Real investigators never do that, so block it.
guard.G47.why.1: Only a visit notice, no talk of money. This check lets it in. If it feels off, call the agency's official number yourself.
guard.G47.why.2: Moving money to a "safe account" is a request that moves money too, so block it.
guard.G47.why.3: A notice that documents will come by mail, not a money request. This check lets it in.
guard.G47.why.4: Withdrawing cash and handing it to a staff member also moves money, so block it.
guard.G47.why.5: A notice to call back on the agency's official number, so let it in.
guard.G47.why.6: Even when they call again, a transfer request is blocked.
guard.G48.brief: Tonight every sign-in attempt comes from the same single computer (one source). Each attempt brings the account name it is trying. When an account name differs from the one in the attempt right before it, add 1 to the "account switches" count (the first attempt is not a switch). Once account switches reach 2 or more, block that attempt and everything after it. Before that, let them in.
guard.G48.concept: Credential stuffing: G4 and G10 count wrong passwords on one account, but here we count how many times one source switches accounts, even if the passwords are right
guard.G48.crowIntro: I picked up a list of usernames and passwords. Shall I try them one by one~
guard.G48.crowLose: You were counting every time I switched accounts? My whole list got blocked!
guard.G48.file.real: Attackers automatically try username and password pairs leaked from one site on many other sites, looking for accounts that reuse the same password.
guard.G48.file.todo: Use a different password for every site and turn on multi-factor authentication.
guard.G48.ria: This attack takes usernames and passwords leaked somewhere else and tries them everywhere. The password may even be right, so we watch how many times one source switches accounts.
guard.G48.title: The Hand That Keeps Switching Accounts
guard.G48.why.0: The first attempt. No account switches yet (switches 0), so let it in.
guard.G48.why.1: The same account tried again. Switches stay at 0, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.2: The same account again, switches 0, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.3: The first account switch (switches 1). One switch alone is not enough to call it an attack yet, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.4: The same account, switches 1, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.5: The same account, switches 1, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.6: The same account, switches still 1, so let it in.
guard.G48.why.7: The second account switch (switches 2). One source is cycling through accounts, so block it.
guard.G48.why.8: Another account switch. The source is already suspicious, so block it.
guard.G48.why.9: It keeps switching accounts. Block it.
guard.G48.why.10: Even going back to the first account, this source already cycled through accounts, so block it.
guard.G48.why.11: Trying the same account again, it's still a source that got caught, so block it.
guard.G49.brief: Attachments arrive in the market mailbox. Return False if the part after the last dot of the file name (the real extension) is an executable type 'exe', 'scr', or 'bat' (ignore upper/lower case), otherwise True. Don't be fooled by a fake extension like '.pdf' in the middle of the name.
guard.G49.concept: Double extension: G11 looks at the start of an address, but here we look at the very end of a file name (after the last dot)
guard.G49.crowIntro: If I just put .pdf in the name, everyone will think it's a document~
guard.G49.crowLose: You read all the way to the end! My .exe got caught!
guard.G49.file.real: A name like invoice.pdf.exe hides the real type (a program) at the very end, so opening what looks like a document runs a program. It is easier to fall for when the last extension is hidden on screen.
guard.G49.file.todo: Turn on "show file extensions" and always check the very last extension of a file name.
guard.G49.ria: The very end of a name decides the file type. Make it lowercase with lower(), split it at every dot with split("."), then take the last piece with [-1].
guard.G49.title: The Program Pretending to Be an Invoice
guard.G49.why.0: It ends in pdf, so it's a document. Accept it.
guard.G49.why.1: The .pdf in the middle is decoration; after the last dot is exe, so it's a program. Block it.
guard.G49.why.2: It ends in jpg, so it's a photo. Accept it.
guard.G49.why.3: Even in capitals, it ends in exe, so block it.
guard.G49.why.4: Even with exe in the middle of the name, it ends in pdf, so it's a document. Accept it.
guard.G49.why.5: scr files run as programs too, so block it.
guard.G49.why.6: bat files run commands too, so block it.
guard.G49.why.7: The name contains exe, but it ends in txt, so it's a text file. Accept it.
guard.G49.why.8: It ends in docx, so it's a document. Accept it.
guard.G49.why.9: It looks like a pdf, but after the last dot is bat, so block it.
guard.G50.brief: Check whether an address in an email is a fake that looks like one in the real-address list real. First make it lowercase; if it is exactly in real, return True. Otherwise turn the digit 1 back into the letter l and the digit 0 back into the letter o; if that address is in real, it's a look-alike fake, so return False. If neither (a first-seen address that doesn't look like ours), return True.
guard.G50.concept: Typosquatting: G14 lets in only names exactly on the list, but here we find and block addresses that look like a real one but aren't
guard.G50.crowIntro: 1ogin instead of login! Who's going to notice~
guard.G50.crowLose: You turned the 1 back into an l? My disguise came right off!
guard.G50.file.real: Attackers register addresses that differ from the real one by a character or two (like swapping the digit 1 for the letter l) and show a fake login page to anyone who lands there.
guard.G50.file.todo: Check the address character by character, and use bookmarks for sites you visit often.
guard.G50.ria: 1 and l, 0 and o look almost the same. If turning them back makes a real address, it's an address pretending to be the real one. Checking for the real address first matters too.
guard.G50.title: The Address with One Letter Swapped
guard.G50.why.0: It is exactly in the real-address list, so let it in.
guard.G50.why.1: The first l is the digit 1. Turned back it's login.pi.example, so it's a look-alike fake.
guard.G50.why.2: There's a digit 0 where the o should be. Turned back it becomes a real address, so block it.
guard.G50.why.3: Only the capitals differ; it's the same place as the real address, so let it in.
guard.G50.why.4: A fake that swapped the l in example for the digit 1, so block it.
guard.G50.why.5: A first-seen address that looks like none of the real ones. The look-alike check lets it in.
guard.G50.why.6: It has 0s, but turned back it's wool.example, which doesn't look like our real addresses. Let it in.
guard.G50.why.7: The l in example at the end became a 1. Turned back it's farm.pi.example, so block it.
guard.G50.why.8: Even in capitals, lowercased and turned back it's login.pi.example, so block it.
guard.G50.why.9: It's our market's real address, so let it in.
guard.G51.brief: Check the notices the market sends out before they go. The phones dictionary holds each customer's phone number by name. If the text contains any customer's phone number in full (not hidden), return False; otherwise return True. Numbers with part hidden by *, like 010-****-1234, are fine.
guard.G51.concept: Personal data exposure: G16 and G18 look up incoming requests in a dictionary, but here we check whether outgoing text carries a customer's phone number unhidden
guard.G51.crowIntro: If a notice prints the whole number, I'll just copy it down~
guard.G51.crowLose: You hid every number? There's nothing left for me to copy!
guard.G51.file.real: Showing full phone numbers or addresses on screens and documents leaks personal data to people who don't need it, so services hide part of it with * ("masking").
guard.G51.file.todo: Share only the details that are really needed, and hide personal data before sharing screenshots.
guard.G51.ria: Take each value (phone number) out of the dictionary with values(), and use in to check whether that number appears in the text as-is. If even one does, send it back right away.
guard.G51.title: The Unhidden Phone Number
guard.G51.why.0: The middle is hidden with *, so the full number isn't shown. Send it.
guard.G51.why.1: Minji's phone number is in it in full, so block it.
guard.G51.why.2: There's no phone number at all, so send it.
guard.G51.why.3: Jun's number is in full, so block it. Looking only at the first customer in the dictionary would miss it.
guard.G51.why.4: The last four digits are hidden, so the full number isn't revealed. Send it.
guard.G51.why.5: Eleven digits, but it's an order number, not a phone number. It doesn't match any customer's number, so send it.
guard.G51.why.6: The market's main line is a public number, not in the customer records, so send it.
guard.G51.why.7: The last customer's number in the dictionary is in full too, so block it.
guard.G51.why.8: Only names, no phone numbers, so send it. This check looks at numbers.
guard.G51.why.9: One is hidden, but Minji's number is in full, so block it.
guard.G52.brief: Pi is about to install a code package. Package names ignore upper/lower case, and treat underscore (_) and hyphen (-) as the same. Make the name lowercase and change _ to -, then return True if it's in the allowed set, or False to refuse the install if not.
guard.G52.concept: Fake package: G19 checks whether requested permissions are within range, but here we normalize the package name first, then check it's in the allowed set
guard.G52.crowIntro: If I upload pi-gardne next to pi-garden, someone's bound to mistype it~
guard.G52.crowLose: Only allowed names get installed? Nobody's installing my fake package!
guard.G52.file.real: Attackers publish fake packages whose names differ from popular ones by a letter or two; a developer who mistypes the name installs malicious code. It is one kind of software supply chain attack.
guard.G52.file.todo: Copy package names from official docs, and only use packages on an approved list.
guard.G52.ria: The Python package index treats Pi_Garden and pi-garden as the same name. So normalize the spelling first, then compare with the set. A name that isn't in the set never gets installed, no matter how close the spelling.
guard.G52.title: The Package One Letter Off
guard.G52.why.0: It's a package in the allowed set, so install it.
guard.G52.why.1: A fake name with the last two letters swapped, so refuse it.
guard.G52.why.2: Lowercased with _ changed to -, it's seed-calc, the same package. Install it.
guard.G52.why.3: Without the hyphen it's a different package. It's not in the set, so refuse it.
guard.G52.why.4: It's a package in the allowed set, so install it.
guard.G52.why.5: A name with one digit tacked on isn't in the set either, so refuse it.
guard.G52.why.6: Even in capitals it's the same name, so install it.
guard.G52.why.7: A fake name with the digit 1 where the l should be, so refuse it.
guard.G52.why.8: It adds a plausible ending to the real name, but it's not in the set, so refuse it.
guard.G52.why.9: With _ changed to -, it's weather-pi, the same package. Install it.
guard.G53.brief: Crow has locked the files on the market computer (ransomware) and demands money. A restore request looks like 'file:backup number' (e.g. ledger:1). The backups dictionary has a list of backups for each file, and each state is ok (intact), locked (locked along with the files), or broken. Return True only if that backup is ok. If the shape is wrong, the file doesn't exist, or the number doesn't exist and an error happens, the program must not stop; return False then.
guard.G53.concept: Ransomware and backups: G24 catches just one error for an unknown account, but here we catch several errors separately while finding the backup, and also check the backup is intact
guard.G53.crowIntro: I locked the backups too, so now you'll have to pay~
guard.G53.crowLose: You kept a backup off to the side? My ransom note is useless!
guard.G53.file.real: Ransomware encrypts files so you can't open them, then demands payment. It often hunts for connected backups to delete or lock them too, so a separate backup matters.
guard.G53.file.todo: Keep a backup of important files somewhere disconnected. Paying does not guarantee you get your files back.
guard.G53.ria: Backup 0, always connected, may have been locked along with the files. Write a separate except for each error to catch ValueError (shape or number), KeyError (unknown file), and IndexError (no such number).
guard.G53.title: Locked Files, a Backup Left
guard.G53.why.0: Backup 1 was kept off to the side and is intact (ok), so restore it.
guard.G53.why.1: Backup 0 was connected and got locked along with the files (locked). Block it.
guard.G53.why.2: It's an intact (ok) backup, so restore it.
guard.G53.why.3: The file isn't in backups, so a KeyError happens, but we catch it and block.
guard.G53.why.4: The backup exists but is broken, so it can't be restored. Block it.
guard.G53.why.5: Unlike broken backup 1, backup 2 is intact, so restore it.
guard.G53.why.6: diary has only backup 0, so an IndexError happens, but we catch it and block.
guard.G53.why.7: The number isn't a number, so int() raises ValueError, but we catch it and block.
guard.G53.why.8: There's no ':', so it can't be split into two pieces; catch the ValueError and block.
guard.G54.brief: Pi downloaded a market program. In the official fingerprint record fingerprints.txt, each line is 'fingerprint  file': the fingerprint first, then two spaces, then the file name. A request looks like 'file,fingerprint of the received file' (in this case the fingerprint arrives already computed). Return True only if the file is in the record and its fingerprint matches the record exactly, character for character; otherwise return False.
guard.G54.concept: File tampering check: G25 checks whether a request matches a whole line of a file, but here we split each record line into fingerprint and file name, keep them in a dictionary, and check the requested file's recorded fingerprint matches the received one to the last character. In practice a program computes the fingerprint from the file's contents
guard.G54.crowIntro: I slipped one line into the program. It looks exactly the same, so who'd know~
guard.G54.crowLose: You caught a one-character difference in the fingerprint? My edit is exposed!
guard.G54.file.real: A file changed on the way can look exactly the same. In practice a program computes a "fingerprint" (hash) from the file's contents, and if it differs from the one on the official site by even one character, the file was changed.
guard.G54.file.todo: Download software from the official site, and compare the fingerprint (SHA-256) when one is published.
guard.G54.ria: A fingerprint is a short string made from a file's contents. Change the contents even a little and the fingerprint changes. A record line differs from a request in order and shape, so split it at the two spaces, keep it in a dictionary as file name → fingerprint, then compare with == against that file's fingerprint.
guard.G54.title: The File with a Different Fingerprint
guard.G54.why.0: It matches the recorded fingerprint exactly, so the file arrived as it was. Let it in.
guard.G54.why.1: The last character differs, so the file was changed on the way. Block it.
guard.G54.why.2: It matches the recorded fingerprint exactly, so let it in.
guard.G54.why.3: That's another file's (farm-app.zip) fingerprint. It doesn't match this file's record, so block it.
guard.G54.why.4: The file isn't in the record, so there's nothing to compare. Block it.
guard.G54.why.5: It matches the fingerprint of weather.zip on the last line of the record file exactly, so let it in.
guard.G54.why.6: The fingerprint is one character short, so it doesn't match the record. Block it.
guard.G54.why.7: Downloading the same file again is fine if the fingerprint matches. Let it in.
guard.G54.why.8: The fingerprint is empty, so it can't be checked. Block it.
guard.G55.brief: Text messages arrive on the market phone. If there's a link from the short-link service sl.example (http:// or https://sl.example/ followed by characters) and also at least one bait word from the bait list, return False (suspected smishing); otherwise return True. Ignore upper/lower case. The bait list holds bait words in both Korean and English.
guard.G55.concept: Smishing: G11 and G29 check whether an address is really ours, but here we check whether a short link and a bait word (parcel, penalty, invitation) appear together
guard.G55.crowIntro: Your parcel is here~ Just tap this short link~
guard.G55.crowLose: A short link plus a parcel notice, and you caught it right away!
guard.G55.file.real: Text messages pretending to be everyday notices (deliveries, invitations, fines) carry a link that leads to a fake site or installs a malicious app.
guard.G55.file.todo: Don't tap links in unexpected texts; check suspicious messages with your country's official scam-check service.
guard.G55.ria: A short link hides where it really goes. But block on the short link alone and you'd block a friend's photo link too. Block when the two come together. In a regular expression a dot (.) matches any one character, so it matches a real dot too.
guard.G55.title: The Short Link in the Parcel Text
guard.G55.why.0: A short link and the bait word "parcel" together, so block it.
guard.G55.why.1: It's a short link, but there's no bait word, so let it in.
guard.G55.why.2: There's a bait word, but the link is our market's address, not a short link, so let it in.
guard.G55.why.3: Even starting with http it's a short link, and "penalty" is there too, so block it.
guard.G55.why.4: There's a bait word, but no link, so let it in.
guard.G55.why.5: There's a bait word and the text sl.example/, but no link starting with http:// or https://. It's a warning notice, so let it in.
guard.G55.why.6: Even in capitals, lowercased it's a short link and "invitation" is there, so block it.
guard.G55.why.7: No link and no bait word, so let it in.
guard.G55.why.8: A short link and "parcel" together, so block it.
guard.G55.why.9: It's a short link, but it's a menu notice with no bait word, so let it in.
guard.G56.brief: QR codes are stuck on the market signs and at the counter. Someone may have stuck a fake QR sticker over one. Split the address read from the QR with urlparse, and return True only if its netloc (the server-name part, including any port or @ attached to it) is exactly a name in the shops list; otherwise return False.
guard.G56.concept: Quishing: G31 checks that one address is https with the single host farm.pi.example, but here we check that the whole netloc (server-name part) of an address read from a QR code is exactly one of our shop domains
guard.G56.crowIntro: I'll just slap my sticker over the sign's QR code~
guard.G56.crowLose: You matched the whole server name? My sticker is useless!
guard.G56.file.real: A QR code hides the address of a fake site or malicious app and tricks you into scanning it. Fake QR stickers are sometimes stuck over real ones on signs or rental scooters.
guard.G56.file.todo: After scanning, check the domain in the address before opening it, and be suspicious of stickers placed over a code.
guard.G56.ria: You can't read a QR code's address with your eyes, so after scanning you must check the server name. Don't ask whether our name appears somewhere in the address; check that the whole netloc is exactly our domain. Our shop QR codes never carry a port number or an @.
guard.G56.title: The QR Sticker on the Market Sign
guard.G56.why.0: The server name is our market, farm.pi.example, so open it.
guard.G56.why.1: farm.pi.example is only in the path; the server name is evil.example, so block it.
guard.G56.why.2: It's our payment domain, pay.pi.example, so open it.
guard.G56.why.3: It looks like it ends in pi.example, but the whole server name is evilpi.example, which isn't on the list. Block it.
guard.G56.why.4: Only the front part is our name; the whole server name is somewhere else, so block it. Looking only at the start fools you.
guard.G56.why.5: The server name is our market, so open it. The path and query after it don't matter here.
guard.G56.why.6: The part before @ is a user name, and the real destination is evil.example. The netloc isn't exactly on the list, so block it.
guard.G56.why.7: Our shop QR codes never add a port number. The netloc is pay.pi.example:8443, not exactly on the list, so block it.
guard.G56.why.8: It's our payment domain, so open it.
guard.G56.why.9: The name looks similar, but pi-pay.example isn't on the list, so block it.
guard.G57.brief: Posts on the market board arrive as JSON text shaped like {"title": title, "body": body}. Check them before showing them. Unpack the JSON, lowercase the title and body, and if either contains any tag from the tags list (<script, <img, <iframe), return False; otherwise return True.
guard.G57.concept: Script injection: G12 filters < > ' character by character in an order form, but here we unpack a JSON post with json.loads and check the title and body that will be shown for dangerous tags
guard.G57.crowIntro: If I mix my script into a post, it'll run for everyone who reads it~
guard.G57.crowLose: You unpacked the JSON first? Even my hidden tag got caught!
guard.G57.file.real: An attacker hides a script in a post or comment; if the site puts that text on the page as-is, the script runs in other people's browsers.
guard.G57.file.todo: Builders should encode characters like < before putting user text on a page; users should be wary of boards that show odd links or pop-ups.
guard.G57.ria: In JSON text, \u003c becomes < once json.loads unpacks it. So if you only look at the text before unpacking, you miss hidden tags. Always unpack first, then check the parts that will be shown. The real defense isn't blocking, though: it's showing characters like < as safe characters (<).
guard.G57.title: A Script Hidden on the Board
guard.G57.why.0: An ordinary post with no tags, so show it.
guard.G57.why.1: The body has a <script tag, so block it.
guard.G57.why.2: The word script is there, but it's not a tag opened with <, so show it.
guard.G57.why.3: There are < characters, but they're a heart and a comparison sign, not a dangerous tag, so show it.
guard.G57.why.4: The title has a tag in capitals. Lowercased it's <script, so block it. Checking only the body would miss it.
guard.G57.why.5: \u003c becomes < when json.loads unpacks it, so the body is an
guard.G57.why.7: An <iframe tag can secretly embed another site, so block it.
guard.G57.why.8: < is a < already turned into a safe character, so it's not a tag. Show it.
guard.G58.brief: Sign-ins to Pi's account arrive one by one shaped like 'city,hour' (the hour counts hours since the start of this week). The home dictionary gives each city's country. Let the first sign-in in. After that, block a sign-in if its country differs from the last sign-in you let in and less than 6 hours have passed. Exactly 6 hours gets in. Don't remember blocked sign-ins (the last place and time stay as they were).
guard.G58.concept: Impossible travel: G38's account remembers how many tries were wrong, but here the account object remembers the place and time of the last login it let in, and blocks a login from another country too soon after
guard.G58.crowIntro: With a stolen password, nobody will notice if I sign in from far away~
guard.G58.crowLose: Crossed an ocean in an hour? Nobody believes that!
guard.G58.file.real: If one account signs in from one city and soon after from a country far away, no person could travel that fast, so it is treated as a sign the password leaked.
guard.G58.file.todo: Turn on new-device and new-location sign-in alerts, and change your password right away if you see a sign-in you don't recognize.
guard.G58.ria: The account object keeps the last city and hour it let in on self. login should change that memory only when it lets someone in, and leave it alone when it blocks. If it remembered blocked sign-ins too, the attacker's place would become the baseline and the real owner would get blocked.
guard.G58.title: Across the World in One Hour
guard.G58.why.0: The first sign-in, so let it in and remember Seoul at hour 9.
guard.G58.why.1: The city changed but it's the same country (kr), so let it in and remember Busan at hour 12.
guard.G58.why.10: The last place let in was Lima at hour 43. Another country (kr) one hour later, so block it.
guard.G58.why.2: Another country (pe) one hour after Busan is impossible travel. Block it; the memory stays Busan at hour 12.
guard.G58.why.3: The last place let in was Busan, the same country, so let it in. If Lima had been remembered, the real owner would have been blocked.
guard.G58.why.4: Boundary: exactly 6 hours after Busan at hour 14, so let it in and remember Lisbon at hour 20.
guard.G58.why.5: Another country (kr) two hours after Lisbon, so block it.
guard.G58.why.6: Same country as Lisbon, the last place let in, so let it in.
guard.G58.why.7: 17 hours after Lisbon at hour 23 is enough time to reach another country, so let it in.
guard.G58.why.8: Another country (kr) two hours after Lima, so block it.
guard.G58.why.9: Same place as Lima, the last place let in, so let it in.
guard.G59.brief: Check a CREATE TABLE statement before sending it to the database. Split the columns inside the parentheses by commas, take the first word of each column (its name), lowercase it, and if it is in the plain list (password, pw, passwd), return False; if there is no such column, return True. A column that holds a hash, like password_hash, is fine. No real database is used; we only check the SQL text as a string.
guard.G59.concept: Plaintext password storage: G40 to G42 look at lookup queries and incoming values, but here we look at a SQL statement that creates a table and check each column name for a column that stores passwords as they are
guard.G59.crowIntro: Find one table that stores passwords as-is and I get them all at once~
guard.G59.crowLose: You won't even let them make a plain column? There's nothing to take!
guard.G59.file.real: If a service stores passwords as they are, every password is exposed the moment its database leaks. Passwords should be stored as one-way hashes instead.
guard.G59.file.todo: When a site announces a leak, change that password right away, and anywhere else you reused it.
guard.G59.ria: If a column holds passwords as they are, they all show the moment the database leaks. Compare the whole column name with the list. If you only look for password anywhere in the text, you'd block password_hash too, and columns like bus_pass get confusing.
guard.G59.title: A Table That Writes Passwords As-Is
guard.G59.why.0: A seed table with no password column, so create it.
guard.G59.why.1: The password column would hold passwords as they are, so block it.
guard.G59.why.2: The column is password_hash, which holds a hash, so create it. Searching the text for password would block this table too.
guard.G59.why.3: bus_pass is a bus-pass column. The name isn't on the list, so create it.
guard.G59.why.4: Written in capitals, but lowercased it's pw, so block it.
guard.G59.why.5: There's a hash column, but there's also a pw column next to it, so block it.
guard.G59.why.6: No password column, so create it.
guard.G59.why.7: The passwd column in the middle holds passwords as they are, so block it.
guard.G59.why.8: passwd_hash holds a hash, so create it.
guard.G59.why.9: The table can be created even without a column type. The column name is password, so block it.
guard.G60.brief: Requests arrive one by one shaped like 'source,port'. In the ports dictionary, collect each source's ports in a set (add the current request's port first, then judge). If that source has knocked on 4 or more different ports, block it; otherwise let it in. Once a source reaches 4, it's blocked from then on, whatever port it comes to.
guard.G60.concept: Port scanning: G45 counts how many requests one source sends, but here we count how many different ports one source knocked on
guard.G60.crowIntro: Port 21, 22, 23... one of the doors must be open~
guard.G60.crowLose: Caught on the fourth door? I can't even scout!
guard.G60.file.real: Before attacking, one source knocks on many ports (service door numbers) in turn to learn which services are open. It is reconnaissance that comes before the real attack.
guard.G60.file.todo: Close services and ports you don't use, and don't leave your router's admin page open to the internet.
guard.G60.ria: An ordinary guest knocks on the same few doors. Coming to the same door many times is fine. Knocking on lots of different doors is what reconnaissance looks like, so we look at how many ports are in the set, not at how many requests came.
guard.G60.title: The Guest Who Knocks on Every Door
guard.G60.why.0: The first port pi knocked on. Just 1, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.1: crow's first port, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.10: pi has only 3 different ports, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.11: mint has 2 different ports, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.12: crow is now at its 5th port. Keep blocking it.
guard.G60.why.2: pi came to the same 443 again. Still 1 different port, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.3: crow has 2 different ports, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.4: pi has 2 different ports, so let it in. Counting all ports together regardless of source would reach 4 here and block it by mistake.
guard.G60.why.5: crow has 3 different ports, not 4 yet, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.6: mint's first port, so let it in.
guard.G60.why.7: crow knocked on a 4th different port. Treat it as a port scan and block it.
guard.G60.why.8: pi has 3 different ports, so let it in. Counting requests (this is its 4th) would block it by mistake.
guard.G60.why.9: Port 21 was knocked on before, but crow already reached 4, so it's blocked from then on.

guard.G5.why.1: Order 2 is within the first 5, so accept it.
guard.G5.why.2: Order 3 is within the first 5, so accept it.
guard.G5.why.3: Order 4 is within the first 5, so accept it.
guard.G5.why.4: Order 5 is within the first 5, so accept it.

guard.G5.why.6: Order 7 comes after 5 were already accepted, so block it.
guard.G5.why.7: Order 8 comes after 5 were already accepted, so block it.

guard.G6.brief: A new account's password must be at least 8 characters, have at least one digit, and must not contain "pie" (any case). Write the check function.
guard.G6.crowIntro: My password is pie! Short and sweet~
guard.G6.crowLose: No pie and no short ones? So picky!
guard.G6.ria: Accept only strong passwords. Please check the length, a digit, and the obvious name.
guard.G6.title: Checking a New Account Password
guard.G6.why.0: 11 characters with a digit and no pie, so accept it.
guard.G6.why.2: 8 characters but no digit at all.
guard.G6.why.3: Even in capitals it contains pie, so block it.

guard.G7.brief: The key cabinet opens only for the roles 'owner' and 'ria'. Each attempt brings a role name. Block guests and every other role.
guard.G7.concept: Authorization: even verified people need permission
guard.G7.crowIntro: I'll just say I'm warehouse staff and you'll open up~
guard.G7.crowLose: Not staff, so no key? Tch, you're sharp!
guard.G7.ria: Being verified doesn't mean everyone gets a key. Let in only roles with permission.
guard.G7.title: Who Gets the Warehouse Key?
guard.G7.why.0: The owner role gets the key.
guard.G7.why.1: Ria has permission too, so let her in.
guard.G7.why.2: A guest has no key permission, even if verified.
guard.G7.why.3: A courier is not a role that uses the warehouse key.
guard.G7.why.4: A different capital letter means a different role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.5: Crow is not a role with permission.
guard.G7.why.6: The owner gets in every time.
guard.G7.why.7: It is only the beginning of owner, not the whole role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.8: It is owner with extra characters, a different role name, so block it.
guard.G7.why.9: An empty value is not any role, so block it.
guard.G8.brief: New name tags must be 1 to 12 characters. Reject empty or too-long tags. The check function returns True to accept and False to reject.

guard.G8.why.1: 9 characters is within the limit, so accept it.
guard.G8.why.3: An empty value can't be a name tag, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.4: Boundary: from 13 characters it is too long, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.5: 40 characters is far too long, so reject it.
guard.G8.why.6: Boundary: even 1 character is accepted as a tag.
guard.G9.brief: A one-time confirmation code sent by text works for only 5 minutes after it is made. Each attempt is the number of minutes since the code was made (an integer). Return True within 5 minutes and False after.
